sections.html:
Sellers here owe a city transfer tax on top of the state one, so judge every offer by what you keep after both. The city also leans hard on building records, and that shapes how smoothly a financed sale closes.

Permit records at the Department of Buildings reach back to the late 1880s, and lenders and title companies pull them before a closing. An open permit or a missing certificate of occupancy can hold up anyone financing the purchase. A cash buyer can simply accept the house as it stands.

Pull together the deed, a payoff statement, recent tax bills and any rental or occupancy papers. That folder answers most early questions from buyers and title agents.

This is a crowded city: 72,304 people on 4.39 square miles, with just 42.9 percent of homes owner-occupied. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $484,000. Rent is about $1,629 and household income is $78,779.

With most homes rented, a lot of sellers own a two- or three-family building, or inherited one. Those buildings bring occupancy inspections, tenant paperwork and sometimes a vacancy inspection. Cash buyers can often step into a tenanted building instead of waiting for it to empty.

The city charges 1.5 percent on whatever part of the price is over $50,000, and the grantor, meaning you, pays it. Chapter 234 of the city code sets a 30 day window running from delivery of the deed, and payment must come before recording. New York's state tax of $2 per $500 comes on top.

Both parties swear to a joint return filed with the City Comptroller, whether or not tax is due. A late payment adds an 8 percent penalty and 1.5 percent interest per month. If the seller is exempt, the buyer is stuck with the bill. Check that the closing statement lists the amount, and have your attorney run the numbers on your real price before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: Department of Buildings and certificates of occupancy
sections.html:
The Department of Buildings works from City Hall, 1 Roosevelt Square, Room 210. It issues permits, inspects work and handles certificates of occupancy. The city says a certificate is needed only when major work or a change in use has happened since the house was built.

To see what the city has on record, bring your block and lot number and read the file. If there is no certificate, you apply for one, and missing floor plans must be replaced by plans drawn to architectural standards. Permitted work that departs from the city's records has to be legalized with a new building permit.

  • A permit costs $80 plus $6 per $1,000 of estimated cost, and it stays valid for a year while insurance is current.
  • Roofs may hold two layers at most before all must come off.
  • Fences can reach four feet in front yards on mapped streets and six feet at the sides and rear.
  • Rental units face a vacancy inspection, and large multiple dwellings can face a building-wide task force inspection.

Work without a permit produces a violation and penalty fees. The owner carries the responsibility for permits even if a contractor files them.

The city bills in two installments, while the county sends one bill.

Mount Vernon property tax due dates
BillDue date
City tax, first installmentJanuary 31
City tax, second installmentJuly 31
County taxApril 30

You can pay at the Finance Office counter, by mail, or through Info-Tax Online, which charges 2.65 percent on cards and $1.50 per electronic check. Before selling, request a current payoff of any open city tax from the Finance Office. The city's payment page explains the options.

The Assessor prepares the roll, records every deed transfer and applies exemptions. Look for the tentative roll by June 1. Grievances go to the Board of Assessment Review on the third Tuesday in June, 4 to 8 pm, and the final roll is set August 1. File a separate RP-524 for each parcel; only one grievance per property is allowed.

STAR works a little differently from what many owners expect. Anyone who applied from May 1, 2015 onward registers with the state at tax.ny.gov/star and gets a credit check rather than an exemption.

sections.h2: Recording the deed with Westchester County
sections.html:
Recording happens at the Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division, which also takes the state TP-584. For fee math, the clerk sends filers to its online Property Records Electronic Portal. Taxes may be paid by ACH, certified check, bank check, attorney escrow check or an approved vendor's check.

The state's return is due by the 15th day after the deed is delivered. The city code wants proof of payment affixed to the deed before it is recorded, so have your lawyer or title agent confirm that the Comptroller has been paid first.

sections.h2: Selling a tenanted or multifamily building
sections.html:
Two- and three-family houses are common in this city, and a tenant does not have to leave for you to sell. A cash buyer can purchase the building with tenants in place and take over the leases. A buyer using a mortgage will usually want vacancy or a clean inspection history first, and that can add weeks.

Gather the leases, rent roll and any inspection reports before you list. If the city has flagged the building for a vacancy inspection or a task force review, resolve or disclose that early. Buyers price in the unknown, and a clear file tends to bring a firmer offer.

Visit the Department of Buildings with your block and lot number and ask what the file shows for your address. Learning about an old open permit in week one is far better than hearing about it from a title agent the day before closing.

sections.h2: What to bring to City Hall
sections.html: A short trip to the Department of Buildings can answer most questions before a buyer asks them. Bring photo identification, your block and lot number, and any old permits or plans you have stored. Ask for the file on your address, check for open permits, and ask what is needed to close any that remain. If a floor plan is missing, budget for a drawn replacement. Bring notes on what the clerk tells you, then share them with your attorney.

Once you accept an offer, the title company orders a search and reviews the city's building file. If a certificate of occupancy is missing, a financed buyer may ask you to obtain one, which is why many owners of older buildings lean toward cash offers. Meanwhile your attorney prepares the deed, the transfer tax returns and the payoff request. On the closing date you sign, the city and state taxes are paid from your proceeds, and the deed goes to the county clerk for recording.

faqs.q: Does Mount Vernon charge its own transfer tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The city takes 1.5 percent of the price above $50,000, and the seller pays within 30 days of delivering the deed, before recording. New York's $2 per $500 is charged on top.

faqs.q: Who files the joint transfer tax return in Mount Vernon?
faqs.a: Buyer and seller swear to it together, and it goes to the City Comptroller even when no tax is due. Your attorney or title agent usually handles the filing.

faqs.q: Can I sell in Mount Vernon with no certificate of occupancy?
faqs.a: A bank and title company will usually inspect the city's building file for a financed buyer. The Department of Buildings says a certificate is needed only after major work or a change of use. A cash buyer may take the property as-is.

faqs.q: What are the city and county tax due dates?
faqs.a: City tax is due January 31 and July 31. County tax is due April 30.

faqs.q: Where can I see my property's assessment?
faqs.a: The Assessor keeps the roll, and tentative and final versions are posted on the city website. The tentative roll is out by June 1 and becomes final on August 1.
